conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re adjusting to life with your new baby. I’ll be using a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale) that simply asks about your mood, thoughts, and feelings over the past seven days. It’s completely confidential, and there’s no right or wrong answer—just whatever is true for you. We’ll go through ten gentle questions, one at a time. When you’re ready, we can begin.

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult for you?
Honestly… I’ve laughed maybe once or twice, but it feels like work. Most of the time when my partner tries to joke, I just can’t find it funny—I’m too tired or worried about the baby to even smile.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
No… not really. I mean, maybe a little chuckle here or there, but it’s like the joy is stuck behind a wall. Nothing feels truly funny anymore.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but lately it’s like I’m just going through the motions. I’ll think “I should want to do this,” but the feeling isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

All the time. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not feeding her right or I missed some cue. Yesterday the diaper leaked onto the couch and I stood there crying, telling my husband it was my fault for not changing her fast enough. I know in my head it’s irrational, but the guilt just crashes over me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be rocking her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not breathing, even though I can see her chest moving. Or I’ll lie awake at night replaying every little grunt she made, convinced something’s wrong even though the pediatrician said she’s perfect. I know it doesn’t make sense, but I can’t shut it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it hits out of nowhere. Like yesterday, I was just warming a bottle and suddenly my chest felt tight, heart pounding, like something awful was about to happen. I had to put the baby in the crib and go sit down because I thought I might pass out. There wasn’t any real danger—just this wave of panic.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most of the time. Between feedings every two hours, the laundry mountain, and trying to remember if I ate today, it feels like I’m drowning. I start one chore, hear her cry, drop everything, and by evening the house is still a mess and I’m exhausted. I keep thinking, “I should be able to handle this,” but the pile never shrinks and the tension in my chest just stays there.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll finally get her down, crawl into bed myself, and then my brain won’t shut off. I lie there replaying every little hiccup she had, worrying I missed something, or just feeling this heavy sadness I can’t name. Some nights I watch the clock slide past two, three, four a.m., and when I do drift off she’s up again in what feels like minutes.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll be feeding her and tears just start rolling down my cheeks for no clear reason. People keep telling me I should be soaking up these precious newborn moments, but most of the time I just feel empty and weepy.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… it’s been happening a few times a week. Sometimes it’s when she won’t settle and I feel like I’m failing her, or I’ll see a diaper commercial and just burst into tears. The sadness feels so heavy that crying seems like the only way to let a little of it out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and cried a lot, but I haven’t had any thoughts of hurting myself.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 2 wk PP visit

Symptoms endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)
- Pathologic guilt/self-blame re infant care (Q3)
- Daily intrusive anxiety, panic attacks without clear precipitant (Q4, Q5)
- Subjective overwhelm, “drowning,” functional impairment with ADLs (Q6)
- Mood-congruent insomnia (Q7)

Pattern: Symptoms present “pretty much every day,” cause distress and functional difficulty; no self-harm ideation reported (Q10).

Screening significance: High endorsement consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features, postpartum onset; possible comorbid panic spectrum.

Risk factors noted: Lack of pleasure, excessive guilt, anxiety/panic, sleep disruption, feeling unable to cope; no acute safety concerns at present.

Plan: Score and document standardized tool (e.g., EPDS); discuss further evaluation, supports, and referral for perinatal mental health specialty.
